summary:
Altai Krai stands under the national framework of Russia, and the sources record no regional deviation: the 2023 prohibition on legal gender recognition and on gender-affirming care, the Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, and the expanded "propaganda" statutes apply in full to a visitor in this region.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out the baseline a trans visitor here faces: same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. A document presenting a gender marker that does not match the traveller's presentation therefore carries direct exposure at any check point where identity papers are examined.

Publicly "promoting" non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is an administrative offence punishable by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeat offences capable of becoming criminal and carrying up to four years' imprisonment. The 2023 extremist designation criminalises support of or activity within the designated movement, and at least 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.

The US State Department travel advisory covering Altai Krai advises against all travel to Russia and states that foreigners found guilty of violating the "propaganda" law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and then deported, and that displaying certain symbols, including the rainbow flag, is a crime.

Enforcement volume is documented by Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025): Russian courts issued 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the "International LGBT Movement" or for displaying its symbols, roughly 98 of them administrative. Since January 2024, 81 people across 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying symbols such as the rainbow flag, and between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges for alleged participation; one died by suicide in pretrial detention, two were sentenced to prison, and 17 cases remain pending or of unknown outcome.

Charges have reached ordinary commercial activity as well. On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three staff of two publishing houses under article 282.2 with running an "extremist organisation" for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes; they face up to 12 years in prison. The enforcement regime described applies nationally and therefore equally in Altai Krai, and the sources report no Altai Krai-specific case.
tangentialFactors:
Risk in Russia is stratified by ground of identity. The UK Home Office note assesses that LGB people generally face no real risk of state persecution on sexual orientation alone, with the exception of the North Caucasus — a zone that does not include Altai Krai. The exposure identified for this region attaches principally to gender identity and to visible expression rather than to orientation alone, which places trans and gender-nonconforming visitors in a materially worse position than a cisgender LGB traveller.

The pattern of enforcement is symbolic and administrative rather than case-by-case: about 98 of the 101 recorded extremism-related convictions are administrative, and 81 people in 98 cases since January 2024 were convicted under article 20.3 for displaying symbols. The practical risk for a visitor therefore concentrates on visible markers, documents and public expression rather than on private conduct.

Comparison with the North Caucasus carve-out in the UK assessment is instructive for itinerary planning: the assessment of orientation-based risk differs by region of Russia, while the propaganda, document and extremist-designation regimes do not vary regionally in any of the sources reviewed.
localsOnly:
Residents of Altai Krai face the same prohibitions as visitors on paper, but with fewer options to leave. Gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited outright, so a resident cannot bring identity papers into conformity with lived gender; trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023; and trans people cannot adopt or foster children.

No legislation in Russia prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in housing, healthcare or employment, so there is no statutory remedy for a resident refused service, housing or work on those grounds.

Administrative liability attaches to residents as well as foreigners: fines or detention of up to 15 days for a first "propaganda" offence, escalating to criminal liability of up to four years on repeat, and article 282.2 charges carrying up to 12 years for activity framed as running an extremist organisation. At least 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Altai Krai-specific enforcement case, regional regulation or regional exemption appears in the sources reviewed; all three items describe national measures applying in the region. Whether any Altai Krai authority has issued local instructions on implementation is unresolved and not sourced here.

The specific symbols the US advisory treats as criminal to display are not enumerated beyond the rainbow flag in the source text, and the boundary of what counts as "public" promotion under the propaganda statutes is not defined in these sources.

The UK Home Office note's assessment dates differ across references in the inventory (June 2025 with assessment updated 11 June 2025; page updated 12 August 2026), and the currency of its country findings as of the current date is unresolved. The outcome of the 17 pending or unknown criminal cases reported by Human Rights Watch is likewise unresolved.
